A beginner first covers about three-quarters of the end with the mouth and blows across the edge to make a sound, then changes the pitch by varying the air pressure. Both hands hold the instrument, with the body angled about forty-five degrees to the side of the player; the four fingers of one hand cover the lower holes while three fingers and the thumb of the other cover the upper holes. Four further holes below are left uncovered and affect only the pitch of the lowest note and the timbre. More advanced players learn circular breathing, breathing in through the nose while keeping the airstream going so that the phrase does not break.

The kaval is an aerophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 421.111.12, traditionally found in the Balkans and Turkey and associated mainly with mountain shepherds; today it is also used in folk song and dance, in ensembles or as a solo instrument. It is a fully chromatic end-blown rim flute open at both ends, sounded at the sharp edge of one end; it usually has eight fingerholes, seven in front and a thumbhole behind, and four further unstopped tuning holes at the bottom. As a wooden rim-blown flute it resembles the kawala of the Arab world and the nay of the Middle East.
卡瓦爾笛琴身通常以木製成，如山茱萸、杏、李、黃楊、花楸；亦見水牛角、波斯蘆竹、金: The body of the kaval is usually made of wood, such as cornel, apricot, plum, boxwood or rowan; buffalo horn, Persian reed, metal and plastic are also found. Seamless instruments are often mounted on a wooden stand to keep them from warping and to keep the bore oiled. In Bulgaria a three-piece form is common, of cornel, walnut, plum or boxwood, with bone rings over the joints to stop them splitting and with metal decoration; Turkey also uses wood, reed, bone or metal, the metal usually brass. The sounding parts and other components are not separately described.
卡瓦爾笛長期與巴爾幹及安納托利亞的山地牧羊人相關。Pat MacSwyney 認: The kaval has long been associated with the mountain shepherds of the Balkans and Anatolia. Pat MacSwyney holds that it spread with the Yörük from the Taurus mountains of southern Anatolia into the southern Balkans of southeastern Europe. It was once almost exclusively a shepherd's instrument, whereas today it is widely used for folk song and dance, as a solo instrument or in ensembles. Different regions developed their own forms and uses: Bulgaria has common alto and bass kavals and a pair played in unison; Romania and Moldova have six-hole, five-hole and near-Bulgarian types; and the Turkish term covers a number of shepherd's flutes.
卡瓦爾笛音色明亮而富有穿透力，具有獨特的鄉村質感。其音色介於現代長笛的清晰與民族: The kaval's timbre is bright and penetrating, with a distinctive rustic quality. It lies between the clarity of the modern flute and the raw feel of a folk instrument, with a warm woody colour and a slight hoarseness that gives the music a plain, intimate character. Its range is wide, spanning more than two octaves: the low register is deep and full, the middle rich and warm, and the top clear and sharp. Because it is open at both ends, it produces natural resonance and overtones, giving it a rich harmonic content. Compared with the refinement and transparency of the transverse flute it is wilder and more forceful; compared with the recorder it is brighter and more direct. Its sound has a strong regional character and suits mountain pastoral song and folk manners.
